# Help Those on the Sinking Ship

> "Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself so that you also aren't tempted."
>
> — Galatians 6:1

You're off the ship. Before you walk up the beach, turn round and look at who's still aboard.

Your brother is on it. So are half the men at your church, most of the men at your gym, and quite possibly your son. From the shore the ship looks different. You can see how low it sits in the water.

## The ship is going down {-}

The men on board can feel it tilting.

For a long time lust floated on one plank: "everyone does it, so it can't matter." That went for the porn, the hand and the conquests alike. That plank is cracking. Men who would never open a Bible are now saying in public that it leaves them tired, flat and stuck. Whole forums exist for getting out. Plenty of hype comes with it, as Chapter 4 warned you. But the man on deck can't laugh off the plain fact underneath: other men wanted out badly enough to leave.

Every man who goes over the side makes the ones left behind a little more uneasy. The excuse was never "it's good". The excuse was "we're all here together". Each empty deckchair spoils it.

Deep down, every one of them knows it's daft. A grown man shuts a door, summons a woman who isn't there, and ten minutes later feels worse than before he started. He can't give you a sensible reason for it. He doesn't feel quite so foolish as long as the fellow in the next cabin is doing the same.

## Why they defend it {-}

So they talk it up. Listen to how men handle the subject. They make jokes in the changing room. They pass on the article that says it's good for the prostate. They shrug and say, "It's natural, mate." None of that is the sound of happy men describing a hobby. Nobody recites medical opinions in defence of fishing.

They lie about it too, mostly to themselves. They halve the number when asked how often. They say "now and then" and mean every night. They have to. A man needs some self-respect to get through the day. The only way to keep it while doing something he despises is to tell himself a story.

And who helps them believe the story? The willpower quitter does. He's the man on day nineteen of his streak. He is grey in the face, snapping at his wife and telling everyone who'll listen how hard it is. The men on the ship look at him and think, "If that's freedom, pass me my phone." His misery is the best advertisement the habit has.

You can be a better one for the other side.

## How to help {-}

Remember what kept you aboard. You didn't stay because you loved it. You stayed because you were afraid: of the long nights, of going without, of failing yet again. Fear is what keeps a man's head in the sand, and you won't get it out by shouting at him.

So don't shout. Take away the fear.

Tell him what it's like on shore. Tell him how good it is to wake up with a clear head and a clean conscience. Tell him you sleep. Tell him you can look a woman in the face and have nothing to hide from her. Tell him you can pray without first clearing your throat. Tell him the shadow has gone and you don't miss it.

Tell him one more thing, because he's sure of the opposite. One pastor says it straight to men like him: "You are not alone in the battle." The man on the ship thinks he's the only one in his congregation. He's wrong, and it helps to hear so from a man he respects. A nineteen-year-old sent his own story to a Christian website for that reason and no other: "I wrote in hopes that someone will read this letter and know that they're not standing alone." A pastor, answering the question on camera, explained why somebody has to go first: "if we don't talk about it in the church no one gets help or encouragement or truth or grace or forgiveness".

Best of all, get him to read this book. It's free, and one link is all it takes: [stopjerkingoff.com](https://stopjerkingoff.com/). Think of his name now, before you turn the page.

## Don't kick a man who's drowning {-}

Whatever you do, don't look down on him.

There's an old belief that nobody is harder on a sinner than a reformed one. Sadly there's something in it, and the cause is nearly always the Willpower Method. The man who stopped by gritting his teeth still half believes he gave up a treasure. He feels shaky. A shaky man defends himself by attacking, so he lectures, sighs and posts sermons at his friends. It may do wonders for his opinion of himself. It does nothing for the man he's lecturing. It backs him into a corner, makes him feel more wretched than he already did, and sends him to the one comfort he knows.

You don't need to do that, because you're not shaky. You gave up nothing and you know it.

Look at the verse this chapter began with. Restore him, he says, and do it gently. Then comes the sting in the tail: "looking to yourself so that you also aren't tempted." The helper is never so far above the helped that he can't end up beside him. A well-known pastor put the same thing in plain words: "We shouldn't beat people up because of their sin."

So never tell a married man he's as good as cheating. Never tell a teenager he's filthy. Both already say worse to themselves, every single time.

## Fences don't free anybody {-}

A good deal of well-meant help makes things worse. It goes like this.

A father finds out and takes the phone away for a month. A youth leader gets thirty boys to sign a pledge card. A husband hands his wife the passwords and asks her to check up on him. A man goes on a mission trip, shares a room with five others, and comes home proud of two clean weeks.

What do all these have in common? They stop the hand, and they leave the wanting where it was.

Ask the man back from the mission trip how the first night alone in his own house went. Being kept from it didn't shrink the desire. All it did was teach him two things. The thing must be precious, since everyone is working so hard to keep it from him. And he must be helpless, since he can't be trusted on his own.

The cruellest version is the one we use on boys. Look at the order of events. First we hand a twelve-year-old a screen and say nothing useful to him at all. Curiosity and puberty do the rest. Then comes fourteen or fifteen, the most confused and pressured years he'll ever live through. He honestly believes he needs it to cope. That is when somebody discovers it and comes down on him with shame.

Some boys can't stop, through no fault of theirs, and carry the guilt into their thirties. Others do stop. They stop for the summer camp or the confirmation class or the girlfriend's sake, thinking, "Right, that's that dealt with." Then come exams, a first job, a first heartbreak. The fear lifts for an evening, the old cue fires, and since nobody ever showed him how the trap works, there's nothing to stop him. One little look. He's back aboard before he knows it.

Your son doesn't need a fence. He needs what you now have: an explanation. He needs a father who can say, "I was caught in that for years. Here is how it works. Here is the way out."

## Pity, don't envy {-}

It's a strange thing. When a man is caught by drink or by the needle, decent people call him a patient and try to get him help. When a man is caught by this, we either snigger or condemn.

Let's take the kinder line. The man on the ship isn't doing it because he wants to. He does it because he believes he can't do without it. Unlike the patient, he gets no clinic and no sympathy, and he usually serves his sentence in total silence for ten, twenty or forty years.

Don't envy him and don't despise him. Feel sorry for him, and then do something about it.

The night Peter was about to fall on his face, Jesus told him what to do afterwards: "You, when once you have turned again, establish your brothers." (Believer or not, it's still the best use anyone has found for a rescued man.)

You've turned again. Now go back for your brothers.
